questions.q: What are the three essential features a cloning vector must possess, and why is each critical for recombinant DNA technology?
questions.a: The three essential features are: (1) Origin of replication (ori) – allows autonomous replication of the vector in the host cell, amplifying the recombinant DNA; (2) Selectable marker (e.g., antibiotic resistance gene) – enables identification and selection of host cells that have taken up the vector; (3) Multiple cloning site (MCS) / polylinker – provides unique restriction enzyme sites for directional insertion of foreign DNA. A wrong answer (e.g., listing "promoter" as essential) reveals confusion between cloning vectors and expression vectors; promoters are needed for protein expression but not for basic cloning and amplification.

questions.q: A student wants to clone a 45 kb human genomic DNA fragment. They choose pBR322 (plasmid, ~5 kb capacity). Explain why this vector choice will fail and which vector type should be used instead.
questions.a: pBR322 is a plasmid vector with a typical insert capacity of only 5–10 kb; a 45 kb fragment exceeds this limit, leading to unstable recombinants or failed ligation. The student should use a BAC (Bacterial Artificial Chromosome) or YAC (Yeast Artificial Chromosome), which can accommodate inserts of 100–300 kb (BAC) or up to 1000 kb (YAC). Choosing a plasmid for large inserts shows misunderstanding of vector capacity constraints — a common error where students focus only on antibiotic markers and ignore insert size limits.

questions.q: You have a gene of interest flanked by EcoRI and HindIII sites. The vector MCS has EcoRI, BamHI, and HindIII sites in that order. Design a directional cloning strategy to insert the gene in the correct orientation. Specify the enzymes used for vector and insert digestion, and explain how orientation is ensured.
questions.a: Digest both vector and insert with EcoRI and HindIII (double digestion). This generates compatible sticky ends on both ends: EcoRI end of insert ligates only to EcoRI end of vector, and HindIII end only to HindIII end, forcing a single orientation. Using only one enzyme (e.g., EcoRI) would allow insertion in both orientations. Using BamHI would not work because the insert lacks a BamHI site. This tests understanding that directional cloning requires two different restriction enzymes creating non-compatible ends.

questions.q: Compare blue-white screening and antibiotic resistance screening in terms of what each identifies, the genetic basis, and a scenario where you would prefer one over the other.
questions.a: Antibiotic resistance screening identifies cells that have taken up ANY vector (recombinant or non-recombinant) by selecting for a resistance gene (e.g., ampr) on the vector backbone. Blue-white screening distinguishes recombinant (white) from non-recombinant (blue) colonies using insertional inactivation of lacZα: the MCS is within lacZα; insert disrupts α-complementation, preventing X-gal hydrolysis (white), while empty vector produces functional β-galactosidase (blue). Use antibiotic screening for initial transformation efficiency check; use blue-white screening when you need to pick recombinants from a background of empty vector. Confusing the two (e.g., thinking ampicillin selects for recombinants) is a frequent board exam error.

questions.q: A researcher transforms E. coli with a ligation mixture of vector + insert, plates on ampicillin + X-gal, and gets 200 blue colonies and 5 white colonies. They conclude the cloning failed because white colonies are too few. Evaluate this conclusion and suggest two experimental modifications to improve recombinant yield.
questions.a: The conclusion is incorrect: white colonies ARE the recombinants (insert disrupts lacZα); blue colonies are empty vector recircularized. A low white:blue ratio indicates high vector self-ligation. To improve: (1) Dephosphorylate vector with alkaline phosphatase after digestion to prevent self-ligation; (2) Use a 3:1 to 5:1 molar ratio of insert:vector during ligation to favor insertion. Also, gel-purify vector and insert to remove undigested vector. The error reveals misunderstanding of blue-white screening readout and ligation kinetics.

questions.q: Design a complete cloning workflow to express a eukaryotic gene (with introns) in E. coli. Include: vector choice, host cell type, DNA source preparation, and a strategy to overcome the intron problem. Justify each choice.
questions.a: Workflow: (1) Isolate mRNA from eukaryotic tissue (not genomic DNA) because mRNA lacks introns; (2) Synthesize cDNA using reverse transcriptase; (3) Clone cDNA into an EXPRESSION vector (e.g., pET series) with strong promoter (T7), ribosome binding site, and selectable marker — not just a cloning vector; (4) Transform into E. coli BL21(DE3) which has T7 RNA polymerase under lacUV5 control for induced expression; (5) Induce with IPTG. Justifications: cDNA avoids splicing issues; expression vector provides transcriptional/translational signals absent in cloning vectors; BL21(DE3) supplies T7 polymerase. A good answer integrates transcription, translation, and host compatibility — not just cloning steps.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Recombinant DNA technology is the process of joining DNA fragments from different sources using restriction enzymes and DNA ligase, then inserting the recombinant molecule into a vector (plasmid, ______, cosmid, BAC, YAC, or viral vector) that can replicate independently in a host cell, enabling amplification and expression of the inserted gene.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you have identified a human insulin gene and want to produce it in ______ for diabetic patients.
What is Recombinant DNA technology? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Recombinant DNA technology is the process of joining DNA fragments from different sources using restriction enzymes and DNA ligase, then inserting the recombinant molecule into a vector (plasmid, bacteriophage, cosmid, BAC, YAC, or viral vector) that can replicate independently in a host cell, enabling amplification and expression of the.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Recombinant DNA technology?
questions.a: Students believe that any plasmid with an antibiotic resistance gene can be used to clone any DNA fragment of any size.

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can design a cloning strategy for a given gene of interest by selecting an appropriate vector, restriction enzymes, and selection method, and can explain how each vector feature (ori, selectable marker, MCS) contributes to successful cloning and screening.
